{{Short description|Concept in measure theory}}
{{for|[[Banach space|Banach-space]]-valued measures|Vector measure}}

In the [[mathematics|mathematical]] discipline of [[measure theory]], a '''Banach measure''' is a certain way to assign a size (or area) to all subsets of the [[Euclidean plane]], consistent with but extending the commonly used [[Lebesgue measure]]. While there are certain [[Non-measurable set|subsets of the plane which are not Lebesgue measurable]], all subsets of the plane have a Banach measure. On the other hand, the Lebesgue measure is [[countably additive]] while a Banach measure is only finitely additive (and is therefore known as a "[[Content (measure theory)|content]]").   

[[Stefan Banach]] proved the existence of Banach measures in 1923.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Banach |first1=Stefan |date=1923 |title=Sur le problème de la mesure |url=http://matwbn.icm.edu.pl/ksiazki/fm/fm4/fm412.pdf |journal=Fundamenta Mathematicae |volume=4 |pages=7–33 |doi=10.4064/fm-4-1-7-33 |access-date=6 March 2022}}</ref> This established in particular that paradoxical decompositions as provided by the [[Banach–Tarski paradox|Banach-Tarski paradox]] in Euclidean space '''R'''<sup>3</sup> cannot exist in the Euclidean plane '''R'''<sup>2</sup>.

== Definition ==
A Banach measure<ref>{{Cite book |last=Wagon |first=Stan |title=The Banach-Tarski Paradox |last2=Tomkowicz |first2=Grzegorz |date= |publisher=Cambridge University Press |year=2016 |edition=2nd |pages=229}}</ref> on '''R'''<sup>''n''</sup> is a function <math>\mu: {\mathcal P}(\R^n)\to [0,\infty]</math> (assigning a non-negative [[Extended real number line|extended real number]] to each subset of '''R'''<sup>''n''</sup>) such that

* {{math|''μ''}} is finitely additive, i.e. <math>\mu(A \cup B) = \mu(A)+ \mu(B) </math> for any two [[Disjoint sets|disjoint]] sets <math>A,B\subseteq \R^n</math>;
* {{math|''μ''}} extends the Lebesgue measure {{math|''λ''}}, i.e. <math>\mu(A)=\lambda(A) </math> for every Lebesgue-measurable set <math>A\subseteq \R^n</math>;
* {{math|''μ''}} is invariant under [[isometries]] of '''R'''<sup>''n''</sup> , i.e. <math>\mu(A)=\mu(f(A)) </math> for every <math>A\subseteq \R^n</math> and every isometry <math>f : \R^n\to\R^n</math>. 

== Properties ==
The finite additivity of {{math|''μ''}} implies that <math>\mu(\varnothing) = 0 </math>  and <math>\mu(A_1 \cup \cdots \cup A_k) = \sum_{i=1}^k\mu(A_i) </math> for any pairwise disjoint sets <math>A_1,\ldots,A_k\subseteq \R^n</math>. We also have <math>\mu(A)\leq\mu(B) </math> whenever <math>A\subseteq B\subseteq \R^n</math>.

Since {{math|''μ''}} extends Lebesgue measure, we know that <math>\mu(A)=0 </math> whenever ''A'' is a finite or a countable set and that <math>\mu([a_1,b_1]\times \cdots \times [a_n,b_n]) =(b_1-a_1)\cdots(b_n-a_n)  </math> for any product of [[Interval (mathematics)|intervals]] <math>[a_1,b_1]\times \cdots \times [a_n,b_n]\subseteq \R^n</math>.

Since  {{math|''μ''}} is invariant under isometries, it is in particular invariant under rotations and translations.

== Results ==
Stefan Banach showed that Banach measures exist on '''R'''<sup>1</sup> and on '''R'''<sup>2</sup>. These results can be derived from the fact that the groups of isometries of '''R'''<sup>1</sup> and of '''R'''<sup>2</sup> are [[Solvable group|solvable]]. 

The existence of these measures proves the impossibility of a [[Banach–Tarski paradox]] in one or two dimensions: it is not possible to decompose a one- or two-dimensional set of finite Lebesgue measure into finitely many sets that can be reassembled into a set with a different Lebesgue measure, because this would violate the properties of the Banach measure that extends the Lebesgue measure.<ref>{{citation |last=Stewart |first=Ian |title=From Here to Infinity |page=177 |year=1996 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=9780192832023}}.</ref>

Conversely, the existence of the Banach-Tarski paradox in all dimensions ''n ≥ 3'' shows that no Banach measure can exist in these dimensions.

As [[Vitali set|Vitali's paradox]] shows, Banach measures cannot be strengthened to countably additive ones: there exist subsets of '''R'''<sup>''n''</sup> that are not Lebesgue measurable, for all ''n ≥ 1''.

Most of these results depend on some form of the [[axiom of choice]]. Using only the axioms of [[Zermelo–Fraenkel set theory|Zermelo-Fraenkel set theory]] without the axiom of choice, it is not possible to derive the Banach-Tarski paradox, nor it is possible to prove the existence of sets that are not Lebesgue-measurable (the latter claim depends on a fairly weak and widely believed assumption, namely that the existence of [[Inaccessible cardinal|inaccessible cardinals]] is consistent). The existence of Banach measures on '''R'''<sup>1</sup> and on '''R'''<sup>2</sup> can also not be proven in the absence of the axiom of choice.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Wagon |first=Stan |title=The Banach-Tarski Paradox |last2=Tomkowicz |first2=Grzegorz |date= |publisher=Cambridge University Press |year=2016 |edition=2nd |pages=296-302}}</ref> In particular, no concrete formula for these Banach measures can be given.
